fullText:
A story about Survivorship Bias and how a young statistician identified this cognitive bias and saved lives:

During World War II, the U.S. wanted to add reinforcement armor to specific areas of its planes.

Analysts examined returning bombers, plotted the bullet holes and damage on them (as in the image below), and came to the conclusion that adding armor to the tail, body, and wings would improve their odds of survival.

But a young statistician named Abraham Wald noted that this would be a tragic mistake.

By only plotting data on the planes that returned, they were systematically omitting the data on a critical, informative subset:

The planes that were damaged and unable to return.

• The "seen" planes had sustained damage that was survivable.
• The "unseen" planes had sustained damage that was not.

Wald concluded that armor should be added to the *unharmed* regions of the returning planes (the areas without bullet holes on the image below).

His profound logic: Where the survivors were unharmed was actually where the planes were most vulnerable.

Based on his insight, the military reinforced the engine and other vulnerable parts, significantly improving the safety of the crews during combat and saving thousands of lives.

Abraham Wald had identified a cognitive bias called "Survivorship Bias":

The error resulting from systematically focusing on survivors (successes) and ignoring casualties (failures) that causes us to miss the true base rates of survival (the actual probability of success) and arrive at flawed conclusions.

Survivorship Bias is all around us — its cost to business can be huge. 

What is unseen often has more value than what is seen.

fullText:
Single class classifiers (machine learning one-class classification OCC algorithms) are often overlooked when dealing with multi-class datasets.

Why would OCC be considered useful? Well, if you try to maximize performance across a multidimensional objective function, you tend to allow larger errors in some classes in order to reduce error in other (perhaps difficult-to-classify) classes. Sacrificing performance in perhaps one of the most critical classes simply to make the overall model look good can be a poor decision. RMSE is an example of a metric that minimizes error over a large range of data, which could be dangerous when the accuracy of one smaller segment of the data really requires higher performance than the rest of the data. 

Example: looking for fraud (a specific category of behavior) in a complex financial data ecosystem (representing many different “normal” behaviors) should receive specific targeted attention. Who cares if you classify with high accuracy all the non-fraud categories during your first machine learning classification run over the dataset. First separate fraud from non-fraud cases with the highest possible accuracy. Then deal urgently with these fraud cases, as highest priority. Then, the non-fraud group of numerous diverse behavior categories can be partitioned with your favorite multi-class classifier(s) according to the organization’s needs and requirements. Years ago, I did some consulting for a large federal agency where we did exactly this!

Similar examples can be given in other domains: acute medical diagnoses, network intrusions, industrial machine predictive maintenance monitoring, environmental monitoring, etc.

See the attached screenshot of Google’s AI response to my query about OCC.

So, the OCC can give you a gold standard classifier to serve your highest priority need first. Then you can resume normal machine learning. 😎

fullText:
Banger paper from Google on RSI.

(bookmark it)

They propose an approach for continual recursive self-improvement at the harness level. They also propose their own self-improving memory system for the harness optimizer.

This clearly highlights the importance of traces and having a functional, adaptive, and structured persistent memory system in your harness.

They show that a harness optimizer improves 9 of 10 continued runs when it remembers why it made each past edit.

They discuss that a common problem shows up when you change the model or the benchmark. An Opus-evolved harness started at 68.41 on Gemini, below the 73.89 of the plain seed harness.

Self-Improvement Memory groups past edits by the harness problem they addressed. For each edit, it stores the rationale, predicted outcome, observed outcome, and evaluation context. The proposer and the selector both read it before making new changes.

Across four domains, including Terminal-Bench 2.1 to Terminal-Bench 4, SIM beats continuing from the harness alone in six cross-dataset and four Opus-to-Gemini settings. Across ten coding runs, it adds 2.36 points on average (p=0.003).

If you evolve harnesses automatically, store the reasons and results of each edit next to the code.
